references.name: Dietrich Dörner
references.tldr: German psychologist at the University of Bamberg who built a theory of the whole mind as a machine. His Psi theory tries to explain motivation, emotion, memory and action control with one set of mechanisms. He was one of the advisors of Bach's doctoral thesis.
references.bach_take: Bach's MicroPsi is an implementation and extension of Dörner's theory. The first chapter of the thesis is a detailed retelling of Dörner's 'blueprint for a mind'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: MicroPsi [22, 23] is an implementation of Dietrich Dörner’s Psi theory of mental representation, information processing, perception, action control and emotion
Paraphrase: title page names Hans-Dieter Burkhard, Dietrich Dörner and Kai-Uwe Kühnberger as advisors; chapter 1 is titled Dörner's 'blueprint for a mind'.
Paraphrase: CV lists joint tutorials and symposia with Dörner (ICCM 2006, KogWis 2005) and a 2008 published interview with him.

references.name: Psi theory
references.author: Dietrich Dörner
references.tldr: A theory of how a mind works as a whole system. An agent has a small set of built-in needs (for example food, safety, certainty, competence and belonging), and these needs create motives that steer perception, memory, planning and action. Emotions are not separate modules but ways in which the whole system changes its style of processing.
references.bach_take: Bach treats it as a serious candidate for a full cognitive architecture and turns it into running software (MicroPsi). He also notes what it leaves out, such as low-level brain details.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: section 1.8 covers behaviour control and action selection with urges for fuel/water, intactness, certainty, competence and affiliation; section 2.3 discusses the Psi theory as a model of human cognition.
Paraphrase: chapter 10 of the 2009 OUP book is titled 'Summary: The Psi theory as a model of cognition'.

references.name: Bauplan für eine Seele
references.author: Dietrich Dörner
references.tldr: Dörner's main book, whose title means 'Blueprint for a Soul'. It builds up a mind step by step, starting from a very simple vehicle and adding needs, memory, planning, emotion and language.
references.bach_take: This is the main source Bach's thesis and book retell and formalise for an English-speaking audience.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: reference [24] Dörner, D. (1999). Bauplan für eine Seele. Reinbeck.
Paraphrase: the thesis says Dörner's theory of the mind is laid down in 'Bauplan für eine Seele' ('Blueprint for a Soul') and that Dörner introduces it incrementally.

references.name: Die Mechanik des Seelenwagens
references.author: Dietrich Dörner, C. Bartl, F. Detje, J. Gerdes, D. Halcour
references.tldr: A follow-up to Dörner's 'Bauplan' that describes the regulation of action in more technical detail and reports computer implementations of the Psi agent.
references.bach_take: Used by Bach as the second main source for the details of Dörner's agent implementation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: reference [25] Dörner et al. (2002). Die Mechanik des Seelenwagens. Handlungsregulation. Verlag Hans Huber, Bern.

references.name: Vehicles: Experiments in Synthetic Psychology
references.author: Valentino Braitenberg
references.tldr: A short book of thought experiments. Very simple wheeled machines with a few sensors and motors seem to show fear, love or curiosity, which suggests that complex-looking behaviour can come from simple wiring.
references.bach_take: Bach reports that Dörner starts his blueprint of a mind from a Braitenberg vehicle and adds mechanisms from there.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: Dörner 'starts out with a very simple system: a Braitenberg vehicle' (Braitenberg 1984).

references.name: Unified Theories of Cognition / Soar
references.author: Allen Newell; John Laird, Paul Rosenbloom
references.tldr: Newell argued that psychology needs single theories that cover all of cognition, built as running computer architectures. Soar is his group's example: a system that solves problems by applying rules and learning new ones.
references.bach_take: Bach uses Newell's layers of description and compares the Psi theory with Soar as one of the 'machines of cognition'. In the CIMC essay the cognitive-architecture tradition is named as background.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: Table 2.1 'Layers of Description of a Cognitive System (Newell 1990)'; section 2.2 discusses Soar and ACT-R.
Paraphrase: reference [16] Laird, Newell & Rosenbloom (1987), Soar: An architecture for general intelligence.

references.name: ACT-R
references.author: John R. Anderson
references.tldr: A widely used cognitive architecture from psychology. It models thinking as rules that fire one at a time over chunks of memory, each with a numeric level of activation, and it is tested against timing data from human experiments.
references.bach_take: Bach describes it next to Soar as a rule-based competitor to the Psi approach, which puts motivation and emotion at the centre instead.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'Just as Soar, ACT-R is based on production rules', but unlike Soar it does not fire them in parallel and allows real-valued activations.
Paraphrase: reference [15] Anderson, J. R. (1990). The adaptive character of thought.

references.name: Marvin Minsky
references.tldr: Co-founder of the field of artificial intelligence at MIT. In 'The Society of Mind' (1986) and 'The Emotion Machine' (2006) he described the mind as a large crowd of simple cooperating processes, with no single principle behind it.
references.bach_take: Bach calls him the most influential recent thinker on the nature of minds and opens his conductor paper with a Minsky epigraph. He borrows Minsky's remark that 'consciousness' is a suitcase word.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Marvin Minsky was quite certainly the most influential thinker about the nature of our minds in recent history.
This has lead Marvin Minsky (2006) to call consciousness “a suitcase term”, a notion that is notoriously hard to unpack.
Paraphrase: listed in the dissertation bibliography with Minsky (1975) on frames, The Society of Mind (1986) and The Emotion Machine (2006).
Paraphrase: The Society of Mind (1985 in the list) appears under modern texts in the CIMC library.

references.name: Aaron Sloman
references.tldr: British philosopher and AI researcher. He argued that philosophy of mind should be done by designing working minds, and he proposed the CogAff scheme that sorts mental processes into reactive, deliberative and reflective layers.
references.bach_take: Bach uses a Sloman line as the motto for his chapter on cognitive architectures and compares Sloman's Cognition and Affect work with the Psi theory, calling it inspiring but not very detailed.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: “Every intelligent ghost must contain a machine.” Aaron Sloman (2002)
Paraphrase: the preface mentions 'Aaron Sloman's inspiring but not very detailed Cognition and Affect architecture'.

references.name: Minds, Brains, and Programs (the Chinese Room)
references.author: John Searle
references.tldr: A thought experiment. A person who follows rules for shuffling Chinese symbols can give correct answers without understanding Chinese, so Searle concludes that running a program is not enough for understanding.
references.bach_take: Bach lists Searle among the standard objections to AI in 2008. The CIMC essay places the Chinese Room next to Leibniz's mill as an illustration of the gap that a functional account has to close, and does not accept Searle's conclusion.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: references [4] Searle (1992) The Rediscovery of the Mind and [9] Searle (1980) Minds, brains, and programs.
Paraphrase: 'Centuries later, John Searle's Chinese Room illustrates a similar gap in his perspective on computational systems', replacing Leibniz' machine with a computer.
Paraphrase: index entry 'Chinese Room argument'; bibliography lists Searle 1980, 1984, 1992.

references.name: What Computers Still Can't Do
references.author: Hubert Dreyfus
references.tldr: A philosopher's long-running critique of symbolic AI. Dreyfus argued that human skill rests on bodily know-how and context that cannot be written down as explicit rules.
references.bach_take: Bach cites Dreyfus for the weakness of purely symbolic systems in real-world grounding, without giving up on computational models of mind.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: symbolic AI 'is also difficult to ground into real world interactions and to scale upon dynamic environments (see, for instance, Dreyfus 1992)'.
Paraphrase: reference [5] Dreyfus (1992).

references.name: The Symbol Grounding Problem
references.author: Stevan Harnad
references.tldr: Asks how the symbols inside a computer can mean anything to the system itself, and not only to the people who read them. Harnad's answer is that symbols must be tied to perception and action.
references.bach_take: Bach's fourth principle says to build grounded systems but not to get stuck in this problem. For him grounding can happen in a simulated world as well as a physical one.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Build grounded systems, but do not get entangled in the Symbol Grounding Problem
Paraphrase: 'Representations in MicroPsi are always grounded in environmental interaction or abstractions thereof', whether the environment is simulated or physical.

references.name: How the Body Shapes the Way We Think (embodied AI)
references.author: Rolf Pfeifer, Josh Bongard
references.tldr: A statement of embodied AI: intelligence comes from the interplay of a body, its materials and the world, so robots are needed to study it.
references.bach_take: Bach pushes back. His fifth principle of 2008 tells researchers not to wait for robot bodies before modelling the mind.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Do not wait for the rapture of robotic embodiment
Paraphrase: references [10] Pfeifer & Stieler (2007) and [11] Pfeifer & Bongard (2006).

references.name: The Language of Thought
references.author: Jerry Fodor
references.tldr: Claims that thinking happens in an inner symbolic code with a grammar, somewhat like a language. This is the classic statement of symbolic cognitive science.
references.bach_take: Bach presents it as the position behind symbolic architectures and sets it against connectionist replies, as part of asking what kind of representation a mind needs.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'The Language Of Thought Hypothesis (LOTH) is usually attributed to Jerry Fodor (1975)', and it tries to explain how a material thing can have semantic properties.
Paraphrase: reference [14] Fodor (1975).

references.name: Daniel Dennett
references.tldr: American philosopher. He argued that beliefs and desires are real patterns visible from the 'intentional stance', and that consciousness is the work of many parallel processes with no inner theatre, so that the feeling of an inner show is a kind of user illusion.
references.bach_take: Bach puts his own conductor theory in the same functionalist family as Dennett and Graziano. He also cites Dennett for the view that the self-as-experienced is a representation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Unlike IIT, CTC is a functionalist model of consciousness, with similarity to other functionalist approaches, such as the ones suggested by Dennett and Graziano
Paraphrase: a compromise between realist and instrumentalist views 'is suggested by Dennett (1991)': beliefs and desires are detected from an intentional stance yet are objective phenomena.
Paraphrase: Consciousness Explained (1991), From Bacteria to Bach and Back (2017) and The Mind's I (with Hofstadter, 1981) are in the CIMC library.
Paraphrase: Dennett, Graziano and Hofstadter are named as people who mean to address the phenomenology questions yet are often perceived as not addressing them.

references.name: Being No One (self-model theory)
references.author: Thomas Metzinger
references.tldr: Argues that there are no selves in the world, only self-models. The brain builds a model of the organism and cannot see that it is a model, so the organism feels like someone.
references.bach_take: Bach uses Metzinger as the detailed argument for his claim that the self is a representation without agency of its own. The 2007 thesis already uses Metzinger's idea of a model of the intentionality relation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'For a detailed argument about why the self does not possess agency but is a representation, see Metzinger 2003.'
Paraphrase: the agent needs a model of itself as a representing thing; 'Metzinger calls this representation a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR)'.
Paraphrase: Being No One (2003) and The Elephant and the Blind are in the CIMC library.
Paraphrase: whitepaper reference list includes Metzinger 2000, 2003, 2021 and 2024.

references.name: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness / The Conscious Mind (the Hard Problem)
references.author: David Chalmers
references.tldr: Chalmers separates the 'easy' problems of explaining what the brain does from the 'hard' problem of why any of it is felt. He argues that function alone does not explain experience.
references.bach_take: Bach and CIMC take the hard problem as the starting challenge and answer that experience is a property of the brain's simulated world, so a functional account can cover it. Chalmers appears already in the 2008 paper's list of objections.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the hard problem, 'coined more recently as a term by David Chalmers', is described as the difficulty of reducing phenomenology to mechanistic interactions.
Paraphrase: Chalmers (1995) 'characterizes this as the Hard Problem of Consciousness'.
Paraphrase: reference [3] Chalmers (1996) The Conscious Mind.
Paraphrase: The Conscious Mind (1996) is in the CIMC library under classical texts.

references.name: Epiphenomenal Qualia
references.author: Frank Jackson
references.tldr: The 'Mary' argument. A scientist who knows all the physical facts about colour but has never seen colour seems to learn something new when she first sees red, which Jackson took to show that physical facts are not all the facts.
references.bach_take: It is the first entry in the reference list of Bach's 2008 paper, as one of the philosophical objections that AI has to face. No detailed reply to it was found in the retrieved text.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: reference [1] Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. Philosophical Quarterly 32.

references.name: Cybernetics
references.author: Norbert Wiener; W. Ross Ashby; Ludwig von Bertalanffy; Gregory Bateson
references.tldr: The mid-century science of control and feedback in animals and machines. It describes minds, bodies and societies as systems that regulate themselves.
references.bach_take: Bach places the Psi theory in this systems-science line. His CV also lists an encyclopedia entry he wrote on 'Kybernetik'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'The description of such systems is the domain of cybernetics or systems science (Wiener 1948, Ashby 1956, von Bertalanffy 1968, Bischof 1968, Bateson 1972, Klir 1992).'
Paraphrase: Bach, J. (2010): Kybernetik. In Sandkühler (ed.), Enzyklopädie Philosophie, Felix-Meiner-Verlag.

references.name: Against Method
references.author: Paul Feyerabend
references.tldr: Argues that science has no single fixed method and that rigid rules of method would have blocked many real discoveries.
references.bach_take: Bach cites it for the warning against 'methodologism': letting the tools you already have decide which questions you ask. This became his second principle, 'Avoid methodologism'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: one should not fall victim to 'methodologism', ignoring what lies outside the methodology already at hand (Feyerabend 1975).
Avoid methodologism

references.name: The Cognitive Structure of Emotions (OCC model)
references.author: Andrew Ortony, Gerald Clore, Allan Collins
references.tldr: A widely used scheme that sorts emotions into types according to how a person appraises events, agents and objects. Many software agents use it as a lookup table for emotions.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it among the many competing taxonomies of emotion and reports that Dörner rejects this patchwork; in the Psi view emotions emerge from modulated processing and are not picked from a list.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: emotion taxonomies are listed (Osgood 1957; Izard 1981; Ortony, Clore, Collins 1988; Ekman et al. 1972; Plutchik 1994); 'Dörner rejects this terminological and conceptual heterogeneity'.

references.name: Global Workspace Theory
references.author: Bernard Baars; Stanislas Dehaene
references.tldr: Says that a piece of information is conscious when it is broadcast across the brain so that many specialised processes can use it at once. Dehaene gave it a neuroscience version with measurable brain signatures.
references.bach_take: Bach treats it as a useful functional account. CIMC's whitepaper says it explains which information is available but that consciousness is the second-order perception that organises coherence among the contents, not the broadcast itself.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: relating perceptual content and knowledge 'is explored in Bernard Baars' Global Workspace theory (1993), and its neuroscientific adaptation by Stanislas Dehaene (2014)'.

Paraphrase: 'Global Workspace Theory (Baars, 1988) proposes that conscious content is distinguished from unconscious processing by its availability to multiple specialized cognitive subsystems through global broadcast.'
Paraphrase: the cognitive-architectures research direction names Request Confirmation Networks, Attention Schema Theory and Global Workspace Theory.
Paraphrase: listed in the dissertation bibliography (Baars 1993).

references.name: Ned Block
references.tldr: Philosopher of mind. He raised classic doubts about functionalism ('Troubles with functionalism', 1978) and separated phenomenal consciousness, what it is like, from access consciousness, what is available for report and control (1995).
references.bach_take: Bach cites Block in his 2007 thesis and 2008 paper. In the 2025 CIMC essay Block appears only at second hand, in a footnote. No direct discussion of Block by Bach was found.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: listed in the dissertation bibliography with Block (1978) 'Troubles with functionalism' and Block (1995) 'The Mind as the Software of the Brain'.
Paraphrase: reference [2] Block (2001), Paradox and Cross Purposes in Recent Work on Consciousness.
Paraphrase: a footnote on Amanda Askell's 2022 essay says 'Askell cites Block (1995) for a more nuanced account of the inner cinema metaphor'. Block is not discussed further there.

references.name: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: A short, strict book that tries to say what can be said clearly, by treating meaningful sentences as logical pictures of facts.
references.bach_take: Bach's thesis cites it for the habit of equating thought with language. The CIMC essay cites Russell's introduction to it for the point that all logic can be built from one operation (NAND); CIMC counts Wittgenstein among AI's philosophical ancestors.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'since Wittgenstein (1921), thinking is generally quite often equated with linguistic productivity'.
Paraphrase: 'As Bertrand Russell anticipates in the 1922 introduction to Wittgenstein's Tractatus', it is in principle sufficient to use combinations of Not-AND operations.
Paraphrase: 'The Missing Institute' text says AI began with Aristotle and continued with Leibniz, La Mettrie, Frege, Tarski and Wittgenstein.
Paraphrase: Tractatus (1921) is in the CIMC library under classical texts.

references.name: Stanisław Lem
references.tldr: Polish science fiction writer and philosopher of technology. 'Solaris' (1961) is about an alien mind humans cannot understand; 'Golem XIV' (1981) is a set of lectures given by a superhuman computer to humanity.
references.bach_take: Bach calls Lem an 'ingenious' author and 'cybernetic philosopher' and reads Golem XIV as an early picture of a large language model that outthinks scientists. He already cited Lem's Star Diaries in his thesis.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the ingenious Polish science fiction author and cybernetic philosopher Stanislaw Lem
Paraphrase: 'Lem's Golem computer is a Large Language Model, capable of running circles around the best human scientists'.
Paraphrase: listed in the dissertation bibliography (Lem 1971, The Star Diaries).
Paraphrase: Solaris (1961) is in the CIMC library under science fiction.

references.name: Developmental stage theories
references.author: Jean Piaget; Jane Loevinger; Lawrence Kohlberg
references.tldr: Theories that describe mental growth as a series of stages: Piaget for children's thinking, Loevinger for ego development, Kohlberg for moral reasoning.
references.bach_take: Bach names them as earlier stage models before giving his own seven 'Levels of Lucidity'. His thesis cites Piaget as a rare case of a unified theory in psychology.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: mentions 'Piaget's famous four-stage model of childhood development, Jane Loevinger's nine stages of ego development, Lawrence Kohlberg's six stages of moral development'.
Paraphrase: 'Piaget's work (especially Piaget 1954) might be one of the notable exceptions' to psychology's preference for small microtheories.

references.name: Five-stage model of personality development
references.author: Robert Kegan
references.tldr: Kegan describes adult growth as five orders of mind. At each step, what a person used to be subject to (impulses, relationships, an ideology) becomes something they can look at and manage.
references.bach_take: Bach says this is the model he particularly likes and uses it as the base for his own seven levels, while not treating it as a strongly proven psychological theory.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I particularly like Robert Kegan’s five stage model of personality development

references.name: Eight-circuit model of consciousness
references.author: Timothy Leary; Robert Anton Wilson
references.tldr: A counter-culture model that describes eight 'circuits' of the nervous system, from basic survival up to mystical states.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it, with Wilson's names for the circuits, as one of the stage models that came before his Levels of Lucidity. He gives no endorsement beyond that.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'Timothy Leary's eight circuits, which have been adapted by the great Robert Anton Wilson'.

references.name: Ascribing Mental Qualities to Machines
references.author: John McCarthy
references.tldr: McCarthy argued that it is legitimate and useful to say a machine believes or wants something when that description helps predict what it does.
references.bach_take: Bach's thesis cites it where he discusses an agent that represents itself as a thing that represents.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: cites (McCarthy 1979) for a self-representation that is intensional and not only extensional.

references.name: Parallel Distributed Processing (connectionism)
references.author: David Rumelhart, James McClelland and the PDP Research Group
references.tldr: The two volumes that relaunched neural networks in cognitive science. Knowledge is stored as patterns of connection strengths, not as explicit rules.

references.author: Giulio Tononi; Christof Koch

references.bach_take: Bach quotes the mill passage in 2018 and again in the 2025 CIMC essay. His answer is that Leibniz lacked the idea of a substrate-independent machine: perception belongs to the software-level model, not to the pushing parts.

Paraphrase: Leibniz's New Essays (1704) is in the CIMC library.

references.author: Max Tegmark

references.bach_take: Mentioned by Bach only as support for IIT, which he rejects.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: IIT 'has been championed by the neuroscientist Christof Koch and the physicist Max Tegmark (2014)'.

references.tldr: German neuroscientist and physicist. In 1981 he proposed that the brain binds features into objects through temporary correlations between neurons, and later defined consciousness as a state of high coherence among the brain's subsystems.

Paraphrase: reference von der Malsburg, C. (1981), The correlation theory of brain function; cited for synchronization theory of binding.

references.name: Illusionism
references.author: Keith Frankish; Daniel Dennett; Susan Blackmore
references.tldr: The view that phenomenal consciousness, as philosophers usually describe it, does not exist; what exists is the brain's mistaken impression that it has such inner qualities.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it as one of six possible stances. His own position is close but worded differently: experience is real inside the brain's simulation, and it is the self that is not real.

references.name: Mysterianism
references.author: Colin McGinn; Noam Chomsky
references.tldr: The view that human minds are not built to solve the mind-body problem, so consciousness will stay unexplained.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it as one of the possible stances and does not adopt it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: option 4, 'Consciousness can in principle not be explained. This is the mysterianist position, which has been argued by Colin McGinn (1999), and more recently also by Noam Chomsky.'

references.name: The Emperor's New Mind
references.author: Roger Penrose
references.tldr: Penrose argues from Gödel's theorem that human mathematicians can see truths no computer program can prove, so the mind must use non-computable physics, possibly quantum gravity.
references.bach_take: Bach disagrees. In his reading Gödel shows a limit of classical mathematics, not a power of human minds that computers lack, and for epistemological reasons our models have to be computational.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'This is the position of Roger Penrose', against which Bach argues that we can only make finitely resolved, local observations and must describe our models computationally.

Paraphrase: Bach criticises Penrose's reading of Gödel in the section on Penrose.
Paraphrase: listed in the dissertation bibliography (Penrose 1989, 1997).

references.name: The binding problem and neural synchrony
references.author: Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade; Peter Milner; Francis Crick & Christof Koch
references.tldr: The question of how the brain joins separately processed features such as colour, shape and motion into one perceived object. Proposed answers include an attention-driven integration step and the synchronised firing of the neurons involved.
references.bach_take: Bach's 2019 paper turns the question around: consciousness is tied to the 'perceptual binding state', the moment-to-moment unified model that attention builds.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'In neuroscience, a similar approach is found in feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade 1980). Another way of achieving binding is called synchronization theory (Milner 1974, von der Malsburg 1981)'.

references.author: Benjamin Libet et al.

references.author: Aristotle
references.tldr: Aristotle's treatise on what makes living things alive. The soul is the 'form' of a living body, its organisation and capacities, with plant, animal and human levels.
references.bach_take: Bach reads Aristotle as an animist in a respectable sense: the soul is the causal structure, or software, of the body. CIMC names Aristotle as the start of the AI tradition, and Bach's 2015 blog post calls his own god concept 'Aristotelian'.

Paraphrase: Bach describes a vegetative layer that plants have, an animal layer above it, and a human soul on top (Aristotle's name was not checked in this passage).

references.tldr: The widespread traditional view that living things, and sometimes places and objects, are animated by spirits that act and experience.
references.bach_take: Bach adopts it in updated form as 'cyber-animism': spirits are self-organising software agents running on living matter. He says he takes it as a metaphysical perspective and not as superstition.

Paraphrase: these thoughts 'led me to adopting animism as a useful metaphysical perspective not as some kind of religious superstition'.

references.author: Harold Abelson, Gerald Jay Sussman
references.tldr: The classic MIT programming textbook. Its opening describes running programs as spirits that live in the computer and are conjured by the programmer's spells.

references.author: John Archibald Wheeler

references.bach_take: Cited by Bach and Sorensen in support of the view that physics studies how the universe processes information.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the idea that information, not matter and energy, is fundamental 'has led John Archibald Wheeler to coin the slogan “it from bit”'.

references.name: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
references.author: Kurt Gödel
references.tldr: Gödel proved that any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency.
references.bach_take: Bach's reading is unusual. He takes the result to show that mathematics which cannot be computed (with real infinities) does not work, and that only constructive, computable mathematics is real. This is his own interpretation, not the standard one among logicians.

classical mathematics that contains infinities cannot be implemented, cannot be real

references.author: Alonzo Church; Moses Schönfinkel; Alan Turing
references.tldr: Different formal definitions of what it means to compute (Turing's machines, Church's lambda calculus, Schönfinkel's combinators) turned out to be equivalent. The Church-Turing thesis says they capture everything that can be computed at all.
references.bach_take: This equivalence is the base of Bach's computationalism: any system that can be described precisely can be implemented on any universal computer. He calls computation the 20th century's most important idea.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Computationalism is the new mechanism
Paraphrase: an unbounded state-transition system 'becomes a Turing Machine, or a Lambda Calculus, or a Post machine, or one of the many other, mutually equivalent formalisms'.
Paraphrase: cites Church 1936, Schönfinkel 1924 and the Turing machine as equivalent models of computation.

references.name: Principia Mathematica
references.author: Bertrand Russell, Alfred North Whitehead
references.tldr: A huge attempt to derive all of mathematics from pure logic. Gödel's theorem was aimed at systems of this kind.
references.bach_take: Cited in the CIMC essay as part of the story of how the foundations of mathematics led to the idea of computation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: Russell & Whitehead's Principia (1910-13) is cited in the section on the foundations of computation.

references.name: Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components
references.author: John von Neumann
references.tldr: Showed how to build reliable computation out of noisy, failure-prone parts by using redundancy.
references.bach_take: Bach and Sorensen cite it to say that a computer does not need a deterministic substrate, which matters for brains made of noisy cells.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: 'as John von Neumann and others note, determinism can be achieved on indeterministic (noisy, probabilistic) substrates'.

references.name: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
references.author: Thomas Nagel
references.tldr: Nagel argues that an organism is conscious if there is something it is like to be that organism, and that objective science seems to leave this point of view out.
references.bach_take: Cited by Bach and Sorensen as an earlier statement of the hard problem.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the issue 'has been described by many others, such as Thomas Nagel in his famous essay “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?”'.

references.name: The explanatory gap
references.author: Joseph Levine
references.tldr: Levine's name for the gap between any physical or functional description of the brain and an explanation of why it feels the way it does.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: Joseph Levine in 1983 'calls it the “explanatory gap”'.

references.author: David Rosenthal

references.author: Stephen Grossberg

references.author: Anil Seth

bach_ideas.name: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
bach_ideas.year_first_stated: 2025 as a named hypothesis (essay dated 2025-09-15, made public January 2026). The underlying claim that a machine could be conscious is in his papers from 2017-2018; that earlier date is my estimate from his CV.
bach_ideas.tldr: The claim is that an ordinary general-purpose computer with enough memory and speed has everything needed to be conscious, and that we can find out whether a system is conscious by analysing or testing it. Consciousness is treated as a pattern of organisation, so what the system is made of does not matter. CIMC adds a working definition: a system is conscious if it organises itself to perceive its own perceiving in a way that makes its overall model of the world more coherent. An 'extended' version says we can search for the right learning algorithm by recreating the conditions under which brains found it. The essay is co-written with Hikari Sorensen.

bach_ideas.name: Consciousness comes before the self (the 'Genesis' idea)

bach_ideas.tldr: The usual picture is that brains first become complex and then consciousness appears at the top. Bach turns this around: consciousness is there at the start and is what trains the mind. He reads the first chapter of the Bible as an old description of this boot-up: first a spirit over the substrate, then light and dark, world and ideas, and only at the end a person. bach_ideas.name: Computational functionalism, and weak versus strong computationalism
bach_ideas.year_first_stated: 2016 for 'computationalism is the new mechanism' (Edge essay). The weak/strong wording is from the 2025 essay. His CV lists a 2014 paper 'Computationalism and Cognitive Science' that was not retrieved.
bach_ideas.tldr: Bach holds two linked positions. Functionalism: a mental state is defined by what it does, so the same mind could run on different material; he sets this against 'essentialism', which ties consciousness to a special substance such as living tissue. Computationalism: any precise theory has to be a computational one. The 2025 essay separates a weak form, which says all formal theories of reality must be computational, from a strong form, which says reality itself is computational. NOTE: the task brief framed this as 'computational functionalism versus strong computationalism'; in the sources I retrieved, the stated contrasts are weak versus strong computationalism and functionalism versus essentialism, so I have recorded those.

bach_ideas.name: Only what can be constructed (computed) exists; Gödel as the end of classical mathematics
bach_ideas.year_first_stated: 2016 in writing (Edge essay separates computation from mathematics); the Gödel reading is stated in the 2020 Jim Rutt interview. A 2015 blog post on quantum computers may be earlier; it was saved but not read.
bach_ideas.tldr: Bach says that something is only real, or true, if it can in principle be computed step by step. Mathematics that needs completed infinities or perfect continua cannot be carried out by any physical process, so in his view it describes nothing that exists. He reads Gödel's incompleteness result as showing this: classical mathematics breaks, constructive mathematics is what is left, and constructive mathematics is the same thing as computation. This is his own reading; most logicians take Gödel's theorems to show limits of formal proof, not that classical mathematics is wrong. He uses it against Penrose's argument that human minds do something computers cannot.

bach_ideas.name: Motivated cognition: the Psi theory and MicroPsi
bach_ideas.tldr: Bach's early work says a mind cannot be understood as a problem-solver alone. It needs built-in needs, such as food, safety, certainty, competence and belonging, that create goals, and emotions arise as changes in how the whole system processes information. cimc.programme_tldr: CIMC is an independent non-profit in San Francisco that says its research is open-source. It describes its method as 'experimental computational philosophy': write down testable theories of consciousness and then try to build systems that implement them, aiming for a minimal working model. Its working definition is that a system is conscious if it implements self-organised second-order perception that increases global coherence. Research runs in three directions: foundational theory (including a project tying Kant's Critique of Pure Reason to computational philosophy), self-organisation and multi-agent systems (mostly neural cellular automata), and cognitive architectures (starting from Request Confirmation Networks, Attention Schema Theory and Global Workspace Theory). It also gives grants, runs salons, hackathons and conferences, and publishes a newsletter.

outputs.title: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
outputs.tldr: CIMC's founding essay. Dated September 15, 2025 on the publications page, announced on Substack on January 16, 2026, and marked as last updated January 15, 2026. States that general computers can implement consciousness and that this can be tested. PDF at https://cimc.ai/cimcHypothesis.pdf.

outputs.title: Did Your Chatbot Just Wake Up? A friendly reality-check from CIMC
outputs.tldr: A public explainer written because people keep writing to CIMC about chatbots that seem to wake up. Explains how language models are trained, calls them shapeshifters and 'really good actors', and says that text about an experience is not the experience.

outputs.title: The California Institute for Machine Consciousness Research Program Whitepaper
outputs.tldr: The research programme in full: operational definition of consciousness, three research directions, relation to other theories, ethics and risk, and an appendix on people. First announced on Substack on 2026-01-30; the text says this version was published April 27, 2026; the publications index shows September 28, 2026.

outputs.title: Prime Hypostasis: A Short Reflection on the Idea that Provability + Hypostasis = Classical Semantics
outputs.tldr: A short Kant-based note on the foundations of mathematics. It suggests that classical truth is what you get when provability is treated as if it were a thing in itself. Also posted on PhilArchive according to the page. Bach is not an author.

outputs.title: Against intrinsic properties
outputs.tldr: A reply to Alexander Lerchner's 2026 paper 'The Abstraction Fallacy', defending computational functionalism about consciousness. Bach is not an author.

outputs.tldr: A three-day global research sprint on artificial sentience, model preferences, AI welfare and introspection. CIMC hosted the San Francisco hub.
